Wine colloids and additives such as mannoproteins and carboxymethylcellulose inhibit KHT crystal growth
'Cold unstable' wine forms KHT crystals on refrigeration; cold stability is defined by conductivity or concentration-product criteria

sources.citation: Cui, M., et al. (2024). Research progress of tartaric acid stabilization on wine characteristics. Food Chemistry: X, 23, 101728.
keyFindings: Excess tartaric acid forms insoluble salts that precipitate as crystals, making tartaric stability a key quality index
Reviews cold stabilization, ion exchange, electrodialysis, and additive methods (gum arabic, metatartaric acid, CMC, mannoprotein)
Summarizes the origin of tartaric acid, factors influencing stability, and each treatment's sensory effect

agave-cooking-fructan-hydrolysis.summary: In tequila and mezcal production the agave heart is cooked in ovens or autoclaves to thermally hydrolyze its storage fructans (agavins/inulin) into fermentable fructose and glucose. Distillery tracking shows fructan conversion rising from 20% to 98% over ~25 h, fructose reaching >80% of total carbohydrates, while average degree of polymerization falls from ~14 to ~3. Cooking also drives Maillard/caramelization and generates 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) plus cooked-agave flavor; excessive heat raises furans and methanol while incomplete hydrolysis costs ethanol yield.
agave-cooking-fructan-hydrolysis.practicalImplication: When reconstructing or diagnosing an agave spirit, cook intensity and completeness explain both the sweetness/fermentability of the must and the cooked, roasted, HMF-driven flavor signature; under-cooked agave means lost sugar and a thinner spirit, over-cooked means scorched/furan notes and higher methanol.

sources.citation: Waleckx, E., Gschaedler, A., Colonna-Ceccaldi, B. & Monsan, P. (2008). Hydrolysis of fructans from Agave tequilana Weber var. azul during the cooking step in a traditional tequila elaboration process. Food Chemistry, 108(1), 40-48.
keyFindings: Fructan conversion rose from 20% at onset to 98% after 25.5 h, with fructose >80% of total carbohydrates at completion
Apparent average degree of polymerization dropped from ~14 to ~3; HMF, Brix, and absorbance rose while pH fell
Incompletely hydrolyzed fructans caused an estimated 6% total ethanol loss at the distillery studied

sources.citation: Ávila-Fernández, Á., Rendón-Poujol, X., Olvera, C., González, F., Capella, S., Peña-Álvarez, A. & López-Munguía, A. (2009). Enzymatic hydrolysis of fructans in the tequila production process. Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry, 57(12), 5578-5585.
keyFindings: Agave fructans are traditionally converted by acid-thermal hydrolysis; a short thermal treatment is essential for developing tequila's organoleptic character
Enzymatic (inulinase) hydrolysis can replace most of the thermal step without major flavor/aroma changes
Demonstrates the direct link between cooking/hydrolysis regime and resulting tequila congener profile

rum-molasses-fermentation-esters.summary: Rum character is set by molasses fermentation and distillation, which together build a congener profile dominated by esters (notably ethyl acetate and long-chain ethyl esters), higher alcohols, organic acids, carbonyls, and phenols. Light rums use continuous distillation and short, clean yeast-only fermentations; heavy/Grand Arôme rums use pot stills, longer bacterial+yeast fermentations and dunder (acidified distillation residue rich in wild microbes), pushing ester concentrations very high. Ageing fermented molasses on yeast lees significantly raises long-chain fatty-ester content.
rum-molasses-fermentation-esters.practicalImplication: Ester load is the master dial separating a light, neutral rum from a funky heavy/Jamaican style; to reconstruct or diagnose a rum, reason about fermentation length, dunder/bacterial involvement, lees contact, and pot-vs-column distillation, since each pushes the ester-to-ethanol ratio.

sources.citation: Mangwanda, T., Johnson, J. B., Mani, J. S., Jackson, S., Chandra, S., McKeown, T., White, S. & Naiker, M. (2021). Processes, Challenges and Optimisation of Rum Production from Molasses—A Contemporary Review. Fermentation, 7(1), 21.
keyFindings: Congeners (esters, higher alcohols, acids, phenols, carbonyls) are the principal drivers of rum's organoleptic character
Fermentation microbiology (yeast alone vs yeast+bacteria, dunder) defines the volatile/ester profile
Distinguishes light (continuous, short ferment) from heavy rums (pot still, long ferment) by congener/ester concentration

sources.citation: Coelho, C., Brottier, C., Beuchet, F., Elichiry-Ortiz, P., Bach, B., Lafarge, C. & Tourdot-Maréchal, R. (2020). Effect of ageing on lees and distillation process on fermented sugarcane molasses for the production of rum. Food Chemistry, 303, 125405.
keyFindings: Three-month ageing on yeast lees significantly increased long-chain fatty-ester content and precursors (C8/C10 fatty acids)
Pot-still distillates retained the lees effect and were more chemically heterogeneous than Coffey-still distillates
Differences traced to physicochemical processes at the liquid–vapor interface during distillation

fat-washing-lipid-flavor-transfer.summary: Fat-washing exploits ethanol's amphiphilic nature: when a fat or oil is stirred into a spirit, fat-soluble aroma compounds partition out of the lipid phase into the ethanol-water phase toward an equilibrium set by each compound's oil/water partition coefficient; freezing then solidifies and removes the bulk fat, leaving a clear spirit carrying the flavor minus the grease. The governing physics: liquid/liquid aroma partitioning depends strongly on lipid-phase molarity, with the most hydrophobic compounds retained most by the fat — why only a fraction of an oil's flavor migrates and trace residual lipids add mouthfeel.
fat-washing-lipid-flavor-transfer.practicalImplication: To predict or reverse-engineer a fat-washed spirit, treat it as liquid–liquid extraction: more fat and longer/agitated contact shift more lipophilic aroma into the spirit, but the most hydrophobic notes stay partly locked in the fat, and a faint lipid residue rounds the texture even after the cap is removed.

sources.citation: Rabe, S., Krings, U., Zorn, H. & Berger, R. G. (2003). Lipid molarity affects liquid/liquid aroma partitioning and its dynamic release from oil/water emulsions. Lipids, 38(10), 1075-1084.
keyFindings: Lipid-phase molarity significantly governs liquid/liquid partitioning and release of aroma compounds between oil and the aqueous phase
Hydrophobic compounds showed a positive correlation between release and decreasing lipid molarity
Lipid solid/liquid phase transition did not change partitioning, supporting why freezing removes fat without releasing trapped aroma

sources.citation: van Ruth, S. M., de Vries, G., Geary, M. & Giannouli, P. (2002). Influence of composition and structure of oil-in-water emulsions on retention of aroma compounds. Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture, 82(9), 1028-1035.
keyFindings: Higher lipid levels increased retention of hydrophobic aroma compounds and released hydrophilic ones
Air/liquid partitioning of 20 volatiles depended on compound hydrophobicity and the lipid fraction present
Provides the quantitative oil-vs-water affinity framework for which flavor notes a fat phase pulls or holds back

acid-correction-organic-acid-blends.summary: Acid correction (acid-adjusting juices and balancing cocktails) tunes perceived sourness by manipulating not just total acid but the specific acid species, the pH, and the titratable acidity, plus blending different acids. Sourness is independently driven by concentration, pH, and anion species, while astringency tracks pH alone — so swapping or blending citric, malic, lactic, and tartaric acid changes the temporal sour profile and drying even at matched acid load. In binary blends matched for both pH and titratable acidity, the dominant anion still shifts sourness (lactic-dominant ~20% more sour than citric-dominant), and monoprotic lactic reads more sour than triprotic citric.
acid-correction-organic-acid-blends.practicalImplication: To replicate or repair a drink's balance, match titratable acidity for total pucker but choose the acid blend deliberately: citric for a bright quick hit, malic for a longer rounder tartness, lactic for soft creamy acidity, tartaric for a sharper edge — and remember matching pH alone will not reproduce the perceived sourness.

sources.citation: Sowalsky, R. A. & Noble, A. C. (1998). Comparison of the Effects of Concentration, pH and Anion Species on Astringency and Sourness of Organic Acids. Chemical Senses, 23(3), 343-349.
keyFindings: Sourness is independently influenced by concentration, pH AND anion species; astringency is a function of pH but not concentration or anion
Lactic acid was significantly more sour than citric acid at comparable conditions
At low normality, acid solutions were more astringent than sour

sources.citation: Noble, A. C., Philbrick, K. C. & Boulton, R. B. (1986). Comparison of Sourness of Organic Acid Anions at Equal pH and Equal Titratable Acidity. Journal of Sensory Studies, 1(1), 1-8.
keyFindings: In blends matched for equal pH and titratable acidity, the dominant anion still altered sourness (lactic-dominant ~20% more sour than citric-dominant)
Monoprotic lactic acid was more sour than triprotic citric; citric was the least sour compared
Neither buffer capacity nor hydrophobicity reliably predicted sourness, so acid choice must be empirical

sweetness-syrups-body-mouthfeel.summary: Sugar and syrups in a mixed drink do far more than sweeten: sucrose raises viscosity and thus body/mouthfeel through extensive water binding, and it mutually suppresses sourness and bitterness (while acid suppresses sweetness) in concentration-dependent cross-modal interactions. The sucrose–citric acid antagonism is reciprocal: citric acid raises sucrose's detection threshold while sucrose raises citric acid's threshold. Sweetness, aroma, and viscosity also interact: aroma can boost perceived sweetness, but higher viscosity tends to dampen taste and aroma intensity.
sweetness-syrups-body-mouthfeel.practicalImplication: When dialing in a cocktail, syrup concentration sets both sweetness and body and partially mutes sourness/bitterness; reducing sugar makes a drink read thinner, sharper, and more bitter, so rebalancing requires adjusting acid and sometimes viscosity, not just adding back sweetness.

sources.citation: Mao, Y., Tian, S., Qin, Y. & Han, J. (2022). Sensory sweetness and sourness interactive response of sucrose-citric acid mixture based on synergy and antagonism. npj Science of Food, 6(1), 33.
keyFindings: Citric acid increased sucrose's absolute sweetness threshold and Weber fraction — acid suppresses perceived sweetness
Sucrose increased citric acid's threshold and decreased its Weber fraction — sugar suppresses perceived sourness, a reciprocal antagonism
Derived quantitative sweet–sour interaction models matching human evaluation within ~1% error

sources.citation: Bertelsen, A. S., Mielby, L. A., Byrne, D. V. & Kidmose, U. (2020). Ternary Cross-Modal Interactions between Sweetness, Aroma, and Viscosity in Different Beverage Matrices. Foods, 9(4), 395.
keyFindings: Aroma enhanced perceived sweetness via cross-modal interaction, stronger in a familiar matrix than in water
Increased viscosity generally dampens both taste and aroma intensity, framing the body-vs-flavor tradeoff of thickeners
High-ester pectin improved mouthfeel without compromising the aroma–sweetness interaction

brewing-water-mineral-hardness-extractio.summary: Brewing-water mineral content is a primary extraction variable for coffee and tea. Density-functional work shows divalent cations (Mg2+ > Ca2+) bind the nucleophilic motifs of coffee acids and flavor compounds far more strongly than Na+, so magnesium-rich water maximizes extraction yield while bicarbonate alkalinity buffers and mutes perceived acidity. The same minerals work in reverse for tea: hard, high-calcium/magnesium water lowers catechin (EGCG) extraction, reduces bitterness, and promotes tea scum/cream, with purified water giving cleaner, more complete extraction.
brewing-water-mineral-hardness-extractio.practicalImplication: Water hardness and alkalinity are silent flavor levers: to reconstruct or troubleshoot a coffee or tea, account for Ca/Mg (drive extraction and body) and bicarbonate (mutes acidity, causes scale); the same drink built on soft vs hard water can taste flat-and-bitter or bright-and-clean.

sources.citation: Hendon, C. H., Colonna-Dashwood, L. & Colonna-Dashwood, M. (2014). The Role of Dissolved Cations in Coffee Extraction. Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry, 62(21), 4947-4950.
keyFindings: Relative binding energies of coffee constituents to cations rank Mg2+ > Ca2+ >> Na+; Mg2+-rich water is most effective for extraction
Na+ binds weakly to most neutral coffee compounds, so softened water gives little extraction benefit beyond reducing scale
Provides a DFT-based basis for ideal water composition and the role of bicarbonate/alkalinity in acid perception

sources.citation: Franks, M., Lawrence, P., Abbaspourrad, A. & Dando, R. (2019). The Influence of Water Composition on Flavor and Nutrient Extraction in Green and Black Tea. Nutrients, 11(1), 80.
keyFindings: High-mineral tap water gave inferior catechin (EGCG) extraction in green tea versus bottled/deionized water, producing a less bitter infusion
Calcium and magnesium promote tea cream and surface scum, degrading clarity and flavor
For tea, softer/purified water improves extraction — the inverse optimum to coffee

mashing-amylase-starch-conversion.summary: During mashing, gelatinized malt starch is hydrolyzed by two endogenous diastatic enzymes with complementary roles: alpha-amylase (optimum ~70-75 C) cleaves internal alpha-1,4 bonds to rapidly liquefy starch into dextrins, while the more thermolabile beta-amylase (optimum ~60-65 C) cleaves maltose from chain ends, with limit dextrinase debranching alpha-1,6 points. The mash temperature program sets the balance between fermentable sugars and unfermentable dextrins, which determines final attenuation, alcohol, body, and residual sweetness. Lower rests favor beta-amylase and a drier wort; higher rests favor alpha-amylase and a fuller, more dextrinous wort.
mashing-amylase-starch-conversion.practicalImplication: To reconstruct or diagnose a beer's body, dryness, and ABV from grist alone, model the saccharification rest temperature and time, not just the malt bill: the same malt yields very different fermentability across the 62-72 C window. A thin/over-attenuated profile points to a low (beta-amylase) rest; a sweet/full profile points to a high alpha-amylase rest.

sources.citation: Bamforth, C. W. (2009). Current perspectives on the role of enzymes in brewing. Journal of Cereal Science, 50(3), 353-357.
keyFindings: Reviews the endogenous cereal-derived enzymology of brewing, with alpha- and beta-amylase as the central starch-degrading enzymes
Brewers exploit differences in enzyme thermostability and pH optima to tune wort fermentability and filterability
Surveys exogenous enzyme aids used to supplement the native enzyme complement

sources.citation: Fox, G. P., et al. (2019). Effect of varying starch properties and mashing conditions on wort sugar profiles. Journal of the Institute of Brewing, 125(4), 412-421.
keyFindings: A 65 C infusion mash produced more total fermentable sugar and proportionally more maltose than a 45 C Congress mash
Malt gelatinization temperature and growing environment significantly affected mash performance and original gravity
Recommends measuring gelatinization temperature because it governs how readily starch solubilizes and converts

brewing-water-sulfate-chloride-mash-ph.summary: Brewing water chemistry shapes beer through two largely separable levers. First, calcium and magnesium react with malt phosphates to release protons and lower mash pH, while carbonate/bicarbonate alkalinity buffers against it; the net effect is captured by residual alkalinity. Second, the sulfate-to-chloride ratio acts as flavor seasoning: sulfate accentuates hop bitterness, dryness, and crispness, whereas chloride emphasizes malt fullness, roundness, and sweetness. Proper mash pH (~5.2-5.6) is required for enzyme activity and clean flavor, while the sulfate:chloride balance steers perceived hop-versus-malt character.
brewing-water-sulfate-chloride-mash-ph.practicalImplication: When reconstructing or diagnosing a beer, the water ion panel is a required input: mash pH out of the 5.2-5.6 band predicts conversion and flavor faults, and the sulfate:chloride ratio predicts whether the beer reads hop-forward/dry (high sulfate) or malt-forward/round (high chloride) at otherwise identical grist and hop bills.

sources.citation: Eumann, M. & Schildbach, S. (2012). 125th Anniversary Review: Water sources and treatment in brewing. Journal of the Institute of Brewing, 118(1), 12-21.
keyFindings: States the Kolbach residual alkalinity framework: bicarbonate offsets the pH-lowering benefit of calcium/magnesium
Identifies sulfate as a welcome calcium-balancing anion limited mainly by its dry/astringent flavor impact
Reviews treatment technologies (lime softening, ion exchange, reverse osmosis) for tailoring source water

beer-staling-trans-2-nonenal-oxidation.summary: Beer flavor instability ('staling') is dominated by the accumulation of volatile aldehydes during storage that take the beer above their very low flavor thresholds, producing cardboard, papery, and cooked off-notes. The iconic marker is trans-2-nonenal, a lipid-oxidation aldehyde with a ~0.03 ug/L threshold long associated with the cardboard note, though Strecker- and Maillard-derived aldehydes are equally important and nonenal can be released non-oxidatively from bound precursors. Key accelerants are heat, oxygen ingress, transition-metal ions, and a high malt heat load/aldehyde-precursor reservoir laid down in malting.
beer-staling-trans-2-nonenal-oxidation.practicalImplication: When diagnosing an aged or 'off' beer, a cardboard/papery profile points to aldehyde-driven staling: check package oxygen, storage temperature/time, metal-ion exposure, and malt heat load rather than the fresh recipe. Predicting shelf-life requires modeling aldehyde formation and release pathways, not just the original ingredients.

sources.citation: Vanderhaegen, B., Neven, H., Verachtert, H. & Derdelinckx, G. (2006). The chemistry of beer aging - a critical review. Food Chemistry, 95(3), 357-381.
keyFindings: Identifies the cardboard-flavored (E)-2-nonenal formed by lipid oxidation as the most-cited staling compound
Beer staling is a complex superposition of formation and degradation reactions, so trans-2-nonenal alone cannot explain sensory change
Synthesizes the chemical origins of aging flavors (lipid oxidation, Maillard, Strecker, ester/glycoside hydrolysis)

sources.citation: Filipowska, W., et al. (2021). On the contribution of malt quality and the malting process to the formation of beer staling aldehydes: a review. Journal of the Institute of Brewing, 127(2), 107-126.
keyFindings: Malt delivers staling aldehydes and their precursors into the brewing process, making malt quality a root cause of flavor instability
Low-staling malt has low Kolbach index, heat load, color, lipoxygenase activity, Strecker aldehydes, and metal ions, plus high antioxidant activity
Adjusting steeping, germination, and lower-heat kilning can reduce the malt-borne aldehyde-precursor reservoir

kettle-souring-lactobacillus-lactic-acid.summary: Sour beer styles such as Berliner Weisse and Gose get their tart character from lactic acid produced by lactic acid bacteria, chiefly Lactobacillus. Modern 'kettle souring' replaces slow spontaneous mixed fermentation with a controlled pre-yeast step: unhopped, low-IBU wort is pitched with Lactobacillus and held warm (~38-46 C) for ~24-48 h until it reaches a target pH (~3.2-3.7), then boiled to kill the bacteria before a clean Saccharomyces fermentation. This works because hop iso-alpha-acids strongly inhibit lactobacilli, so souring must precede hopping; it yields a fast, consistent, predominantly lactic clean sour.
kettle-souring-lactobacillus-lactic-acid.practicalImplication: To reconstruct or diagnose a sour beer, the lactic acidity and final pH are explained by a discrete Lactobacillus acidification step (timing, temperature, IBU level), not by the yeast. A clean single-note tartness with low funk indicates kettle souring; a stalled or under-sour result usually traces to hop iso-alpha-acid inhibition or insufficient time/temperature.

sources.citation: Dysvik, A., La Rosa, S. L., De Rouck, G., Rukke, E.-O., Westereng, B. & Wicklund, T. (2020). Microbial Dynamics in Traditional and Modern Sour Beer Production. Applied and Environmental Microbiology, 86(14), e00566-20.
keyFindings: Reviews lactobacilli as the primary agents generating the high lactic/acetic organic-acid load and reduced pH of sour beers
Contrasts slow spontaneous souring with modern biological acidification (sour mash, kettle sour) using selected LAB cultures
Pre-fermentation LAB acidification of unhopped wort circumvents the inhibitory hurdles (iso-alpha-acids, ethanol, low pH)

dry-hopping-biotransformation-hop-creep.summary: Dry-hopping adds hops to fermenting or conditioning beer to extract aroma, but it triggers two distinct phenomena. Biotransformation: live yeast enzymatically convert hop-derived precursors into more aromatic compounds (beta-glucosidase release of bound terpene alcohols like linalool and geraniol; beta-lyase release of fruity thiols; reduction of geraniol to citronellol), reshaping the hop aroma rather than just extracting it. Hop creep: hops carry amylolytic enzymes (notably beta-amylase) that hydrolyze residual dextrins into fermentable sugars, causing unwanted secondary fermentation, super-attenuation, higher ABV, diacetyl off-flavor, and dangerous over-carbonation of packaged beer.
dry-hopping-biotransformation-hop-creep.practicalImplication: Reconstructing a dry-hopped beer's aroma requires modeling yeast biotransformation, not just the hop oil profile, because the same hops produce different aromatics depending on yeast and dosing timing. A dry-hopped beer that finishes drier/stronger than its recipe, gushes, or shows buttery diacetyl is diagnostic of hop creep, and packaging-safety risk should be flagged.

sources.citation: Klimczak, K. & Cioch-Skoneczny, M. (2023). Effects of Dry-Hopping on Beer Chemistry and Sensory Properties - A Review. Molecules, 28(18), 6648.
keyFindings: Glycosidically bound terpene alcohols (linalool, alpha-terpineol, citronellol, geraniol) can be released by yeast beta-glucosidase during dry-hopping to intensify citrusy aroma
Bound terpene glycosides occur largely as pentose-hexose-monoterpenols, implicating additional enzyme activities
Documents hop-variety and process dependence of aroma transfer

sources.citation: Svedlund, N., Evering, S., Gibson, B. & Krogerus, K. (2022). Fruits of their labour: biotransformation reactions of yeasts during brewery fermentation. Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology, 106(13-16), 4929-4944.
keyFindings: Reviews yeast biotransformation: beta-lyase liberation of polyfunctional thiols and beta-glucosidase release of bound terpene alcohols
Describes isomerization/reduction such as geraniol (rose) to beta-citronellol (citrus)
Frames biotransformation as a route to greater flavor control and raw-material efficiency

sources.citation: Bruner, J., Marcus, A. & Fox, G. (2021). Dry-Hop Creep Potential of Various Saccharomyces Yeast Species and Strains. Fermentation, 7(2), 66.
keyFindings: Hops contain enzymes that hydrolyze unfermentable dextrins into fermentable sugars, causing over-attenuation ('hop creep') with live yeast
Across 30 Saccharomyces strains, real degree of fermentation was significantly higher in dry-hopped fermentations
No yeast reliably mitigated dry-hop creep; pH shifted significantly after dry-hopping

malt-kilning-maillard-color-flavor.summary: Malt color and much of its flavor are generated non-enzymatically during the kilning/curing and roasting stages, primarily by the Maillard reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars, with caramelization and pyrolysis adding in at higher heat. Below ~85 C drying mainly preserves enzymes (pale malt); as curing temperature rises above ~100 C, Maillard chemistry accelerates to produce Strecker aldehydes (malty, bready, nutty aromas), heterocyclic flavor compounds, and melanoidins responsible for deep color. End-temperature is the key control variable: maximal browning occurs roughly between 125-160 C, and intensive roasting (~157-166 C) drives the high-molecular-weight melanoidins that define dark malts.
malt-kilning-maillard-color-flavor.practicalImplication: When reconstructing or diagnosing a beer's color and toasty/caramel/roast character, the malt's kiln/roast end-temperature and curing time are the controlling levers, not merely which named malt is on the bill. A beer darker or more melanoidin-rich than expected points to higher kilning intensity; pale, clean, enzyme-rich character points to gentle sub-85 C drying.

sources.citation: Prado, R., Gastl, M. & Becker, T. (2021). Aroma and color development during the production of specialty malts: A review. Comprehensive Reviews in Food Science and Food Safety, 20(5), 4816-4840.
keyFindings: Curing above ~85 C intensifies Maillard reactions producing volatiles, melanoidins, and non-fermentable dextrins, while pale malt is dried gently
Specialty malts use higher curing temperatures and controlled moisture to drive Maillard products that set malt flavor and color
Higher kilning intensity lowers nonenal potential but raises other stale-related aldehydes and sweet-aroma furanones

sources.citation: Coghe, S., Gheeraert, B., Michiels, A. & Delvaux, F. R. (2006). Development of Maillard Reaction Related Characteristics During Malt Roasting. Journal of the Institute of Brewing, 112(2), 148-156.
keyFindings: Identifies attained end-temperature as the key parameter controlling non-enzymatic browning, with maximal browning between ~125 and 160 C
Color-formation rate during mild roasting differs sharply from intensive roasting
High-molecular-weight melanoidins are generated mainly by intensive roasting (~157-166 C)
